title: Why Does My House Smell Like Gas?

seo.title: Why Does My House Smell Like Gas?

seo.search_intent: Identify the most likely causes behind “Why Does My House Smell Like Gas,” use distinguishing clues, and decide what to check first and when to get help.

content_html:
If a home smells like fuel gas, the priority is not finding the leak; it is leaving. Distributed gas is typically odorized so leaks are noticeable. If you clearly smell gas or hear leaking, avoid switches, flames, and phones indoors, evacuate, and contact the gas utility or emergency services from outside.

If the odor is clear, leave without operating electrical devices

Do not turn lights, fans, appliances, or plugs on or off, and do not search for the source by approaching appliances. Get people and pets outside and move away from the building.

Call the appropriate service from outside

Contact the gas utility or emergency services according to the severity of the situation and local guidance. Do not re-enter until authorized personnel say it is safe.

A carbon monoxide alarm does not replace this response

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a different gas and has no odor. A CO alarm is important for combustion hazards, but you should not wait for it to sound before responding to a fuel-gas odor.

If fuel gas is ruled out, investigate other odors separately

Sewer gas, sulfur compounds in water, overheated materials, or some chemicals can create similar odors. Investigate those only after a possible fuel-gas leak has been safely ruled out.

faq.answer: Do not turn lights, fans, appliances, or plugs on or off, and do not search for the source by approaching appliances. Get people and pets outside and move away from the building.

faq.answer: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a different gas and has no odor. A CO alarm is important for combustion hazards, but you should not wait for it to sound before responding to a fuel-gas odor.
